title: Zechariah 5:5–11
context: Zechariah 5:5–11 is the seventh night vision in the common count. The interpreting angel shows the prophet an ephah basket, a container sized to a dry measure, and explains it as “their appearance in all the land”, a phrase readers take in more than one way (5:6). A lead cover is lifted, showing a woman sitting inside, and the angel says, “This is Wickedness”; he throws her back into the basket and seals it with the lead weight (5:7–8). Two women with wings like the wings of a stork, the wind in their wings, lift the basket between earth and sky and carry it to the land of Shinar, where a house will be built and the basket set in its own place (5:9–11). Shinar is the setting of Babel in Genesis 11:2 and the land to which Nebuchadnezzar carried the temple vessels in Daniel 1:2, so many readers take it as Babylon, the place of exile, and some hear temple language in the house prepared for Wickedness. Why the figure is a woman, and what the stork-winged women stand for, are uncertain. The Hebrew word for wickedness is feminine, which may explain the figure. The stork is listed among unclean birds in Leviticus 11:19, which some readers think fits the errand, while others see only strong wings suited to a long flight; the vision does not explain them. Revelation 17–18 pictures Babylon the great as a woman under judgment; the passages are named here side by side without harmonizing them. Historic, symbolic, and future readings appear in both traditions. Shared ground: the LORD removes wickedness from the land he has restored.

verses.text: Then the angel who talked with me came forward and said to me, “Lift up now your eyes and see what this is that is appearing.”
verses.arminianNotes: The interpreting angel comes forward and tells the prophet to lift up his eyes and see what is appearing. Arminian readers note the angel’s initiative in leading the prophet to the next vision, and they see the visions as a sequence that moves from cleansing toward the removal of wickedness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same initiative and read the sequence as God’s ordered plan for purifying his people. Shared ground: both traditions read 5:1–11 as two visions dealing with sin in the land after the restoration promises of chapters 3–4.

verses.text: I said, “What is it?” He said, “This is the ephah basket that is appearing.” He said moreover, “This is their appearance in all the land—
verses.arminianNotes: The angel names the object as an ephah basket and says, “This is their appearance in all the land”. Arminian readers note that the ephah was a measure used in trade, and some connect it with dishonest dealing, a reading that remains uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the phrase their appearance is taken in more than one way, often as the people’s sin seen throughout the land. Shared ground: both traditions read the basket as a container for evil that the LORD is about to remove from the land he has restored.

verses.text: and behold, a lead cover weighing one talent was lifted up—and there was a woman sitting in the middle of the ephah basket.”
verses.arminianNotes: A lead cover weighing one talent is lifted, and a woman is seen sitting in the middle of the ephah basket. Arminian readers note the heavy lid as a sign that what is inside must be firmly held, and they read the woman as a personification rather than a literal person.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the same scene as a personification, and some note that the Hebrew word for wickedness is feminine, which may explain the figure. Shared ground: both traditions read the woman as a symbol, and both hedge any further identification of her.

verses.text: He said, “This is Wickedness;” and he threw her down into the middle of the ephah basket; and he threw the lead weight on its mouth.
verses.arminianNotes: The angel says, “This is Wickedness”, throws her back into the basket, and seals it with the lead weight. Arminian readers see wickedness actively restrained, and they hear assurance that evil, however active, is not beyond God’s power to confine and remove.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same restraint and read it as God’s sovereign control over evil, which he confines and removes. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the LORD dealing decisively with wickedness in the land; on God and hostile agents more broadly, see the Judges 9:23 box.

verses.text: Then I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, there were two women; and the wind was in their wings. Now they had wings like the wings of a stork, and they lifted up the ephah basket between earth and the sky.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet sees two women with wings like the wings of a stork, the wind in their wings, lifting the basket between earth and sky. Arminian readers note the uncertainty: the stork is unclean in Leviticus 11:19, which may fit carrying wickedness, or its strong wings may simply fit a long flight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same uncertainty and read the women as agents of the LORD’s removal of evil, whatever their precise meaning. Shared ground: both traditions hedge the identity of the stork-winged women and focus on the basket being carried away from the land.

verses.text: Then I said to the angel who talked with me, “Where are these carrying the ephah basket?”
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet asks the interpreting angel where the women are carrying the ephah basket. Arminian readers note that the question draws attention to destination, and they see the point of the vision in where wickedness ends up, far away from the land the LORD has cleansed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same focus and read the destination as part of God’s ordered judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the question as preparing for the answer in 5:11, and both see removal from the restored land as the heart of the vision.

verses.text: He said to me, “To build her a house in the land of Shinar. When it is prepared, she will be set there in her own place.”
verses.arminianNotes: The angel answers that they will build her a house in the land of Shinar, where she will be set in her own place. Arminian readers note that Shinar recalls Babel in Genesis 11:2 and Babylon in Daniel 1:2, and they see wickedness sent back to the land of exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same background and that some hear temple language in the prepared house. Revelation 17–18 pictures Babylon the great as a woman under judgment, named here without harmonizing; historic, symbolic, and future readings of Shinar appear in both traditions.
